column1: # Hard cases for stage 1, and what a voice should say.
# Scored by eval/eval_normalization.py, through the WebAssembly build the demo
# page actually loads, with --style phone (the reading a voice gives a form
# rather than the one a page does).
# HOW THE EXPECTED COLUMN WAS WRITTEN. By reading each input aloud and writing
# down what came out, before running Sayso on it. That matters: a case file
# generated from the system under test can only ever agree with it. Where the
# two disagree, eval/results/normalization.json records the row and the
# repository's failure table says which of the two is wrong, and three of the
# categories below exist because a probe found a weakness and this file was then
# written to measure it rather than to flatter it.
# TWO CONVENTIONS ARE BORROWED RATHER THAN JUDGED, because they are matters of
# style that speech does not distinguish, and testing them would measure
# agreement about formatting instead of about normalisation:
#   - Case. Month names are lowercase ("march fourteenth"); a proper noun keeps
#     its capital, and an expansion inherits one when it has become part of a
#     name ("Reading Road", "Doctor Lee") and not otherwise ("fifth avenue").
#     forty-two", not "nine hundred and forty two".
# Everything else -- which words, in what order, and whether a number is a
# quantity or a string of digits -- is this file's own judgement.
# WHAT IS NOT HERE. Nothing testing the inverse direction: the demo only speaks.
# Nothing where I could not decide what the right answer was; an uncertain row
# DATE. Every written shape should reach one spoken form, which is the property
# that makes the inverse direction well defined.
